column12: the weakness here is that the ratio is not flat across the CMS series: 0.228 (2020), 0.372, 0.367, 0.443, 0.486 (2024). Caplyta's Part D beneficiary count rose from 3,291 to 27,010 over those five years, so in every one of them a large share of beneficiaries started part way through the year and the measured ratio is biased low. 0.5145 is therefore an upper bound on true annual discontinuation and should keep falling as the launch matures. column11: the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network identified autism spectrum disorder in 32.2 per 1,000 children aged 8 years across 16 US sites in 2022, 1 in 31 (Shaw KA et al., 'Prevalence and Early Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Among Children Aged 4 and 8 Years', MMWR Surveill Summ 2025;74(SS-2):1-25, doi:10.15585/mmwr.ss7402a1). Applied to the 54,533,406 US residents aged 5 to 17 on 1 July 2024 (Census Bureau national population estimates by single year of age and sex, vintage 2024, file nc-est2024-agesex-res, which also gives the 340,110,988 total the book's DLBCL rows use): 54,533,406 x 0.0322 = 1,755,976 children. 5 to 17 is the age range both Phase 3 studies enrol (NCT06706674, NCT06690398)
column12: the 32.2 per 1,000 rate is measured in 8-year-olds and applied across the whole 5 to 17 band. ADDM's own rate in 4-year-olds is lower, so the rate overstates the youngest years; identification has risen at every survey round since 2000, so it understates the oldest years, who were counted under earlier criteria. column11: the same ADDM rate of 32.2 per 1,000 applied to the 3,880,536 US residents aged 5 on 1 July 2024 (Census Bureau, nc-est2024-agesex-res): 124,953 children reach the studies' lower age limit with autism spectrum disorder each year. That is the yearly inflow to the 5 to 17 stock above, and because it is 7% of that stock the patients not started in a year largely stay eligible the next, which is what a chronic paediatric population looks like

column11: the share of autistic children with irritability. A scoping review of the published literature puts the reported prevalence of irritability in autism at 19% to 80% across studies, depending on the sample and the measurement tool used (Alatrash S, Paul T, Carbone J, Penner M, Roshan Fekr A, Kushki A, 'Predictors of irritability in pediatric autistic populations: a scoping review', Front Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2024;3:1393231, doi:10.3389/frcha.2024.1393231). The low end of that range is taken: 1,755,976 x 0.19 = 333,635 children
column12: a four-fold published range, and the low end is taken deliberately rather than the midpoint. Both Phase 3 studies require an Aberrant Behavior Checklist irritability subscale score above 18 and a CGI-S above 4 at screening and baseline (NCT06706674 eligibility criteria), which is the severe end of that spectrum, so even 19% is more likely high than low for the trial-defined population. No filter for treatment-seeking or for prior antipsychotic failure is applied on top, which pushes the same way

column11: a judgement. Risperidone and aripiprazole are both FDA-approved for irritability associated with autistic disorder and both are generic, so lumateperone would be entering a market that is already treated rather than creating one, and would have to win on tolerability. That is the case the programme is built on: CAPLYTA's label reports weight and metabolic changes close to placebo in its adult studies (USPI, accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/209500s016lbl.pdf)
column12: the case for lower: two generic antipsychotics already hold this indication, paediatric antipsychotic prescribing is conservative, and no long-term paediatric safety read-out exists before NCT06229210 completes in 2032. The case for higher: metabolic burden is the reason families stop risperidone and aripiprazole, and a tolerability-led branded entrant in paediatric psychiatry has taken more than a tenth of a generic market before. Settled by years of sales, not by an event
